```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, dpi = 150)
```

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)
library(tidybayes)
source("load_human_data.R")
```

Ported from `CoNLL-2025-paper/Scripts/human-prefs-analysis.Rmd`. The model
specifications follow that script closely so results are comparable; the data
loading is rewritten for Pavlovia output (see `load_human_data.R`).

Two differences from the source script are worth stating up front:

- **`participant` is the real identifier.** The CoNLL script built one with
  `group_by(ResponseId) %>% mutate(participant = sample(1:1000, size = 1))`,
  which draws with replacement and so can collide, silently pooling two people
  into one. Pavlovia gives us a genuine participant id, so we use it.
- **`Icon` is dropped from the constraint model.** Every novel item here is coded
  `Icon = 0`, so it has no variance and cannot be estimated. It remains in the
  AbsPref formula, where it contributes zero.

```{r config}
DATA_DIR   <- "../Data/human-responses"   # drop Pavlovia .csv files here
MIN_CHECKS <- 8                           # of 10 attention checks
ITER <- 6000; WARMUP <- 3000; CHAINS <- 4; CORES <- 4
SEED <- 964

## Sum coding for every factor that enters a model matrix, so the intercept is
## the grand mean rather than the value at some arbitrary reference level. Set
## at the top of every analysis script in this project, whether or not the
## current models happen to contain a factor.
##
## Both slots: the first applies to unordered factors, the second to ordered
## ones (R defaults those to contr.poly). Sum coding in both so an ordered
## factor cannot quietly arrive with polynomial contrasts instead.
options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.sum"))

## brms reads models back from `file=` without refitting, so a model cached
## before this option was set keeps its old parameterisation. Delete the files
## in models/ to re-estimate under sum coding.
set.seed(SEED)
```

# Data

```{r load}
d <- load_human_data(DATA_DIR, min_checks = MIN_CHECKS)
trials <- d$trials
```

```{r describe}
tibble(
  quantity = c("participants retained", "participants excluded",
               "novel-item trials", "distinct items judged",
               "median judgements per item"),
  value = c(
    nlevels(trials$participant),
    nrow(d$excluded),
    nrow(trials),
    n_distinct(trials$item_id),
    median(count(trials, item_id)$n)
  )
) %>% knitr::kable()
```

```{r exclusions}
## Two grounds for exclusion, and they are not interchangeable. The attention
## check is about the participant; the pilot exclusion is about the build they
## saw. The two pilot participants (PILOT_PARTICIPANTS, defined in
## load_human_data.R) ran before side counterbalancing existed, so alpha_side is
## NA for them. Keeping them would force the side term out of the model for
## everyone, since the rows with NA would be dropped from the fit.
if (nrow(d$excluded)) {
  d$excluded %>%
    select(participant, n_correct, n_checks, reason) %>%
    arrange(reason, participant) %>%
    knitr::kable(caption = "Excluded participants and why.")
} else {
  knitr::kable(tibble(note = "no participants excluded"))
}
```

```{r side-coverage}
## Should be 0 once the pilot is out. Anything above 0 means some retained
## participant has no side logged, which would silently shrink the side model.
tibble(
  `retained trials`        = nrow(trials),
  `missing alpha_side`     = sum(is.na(trials$alpha_side)),
  `side modellable`        = !all(is.na(trials$alpha_side)) &&
                             n_distinct(na.omit(trials$alpha_side)) > 1
) %>% knitr::kable()
```

## Attention checks

```{r checks}
d$checks %>%
  group_by(item_id, Alpha, expected) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), pct_correct = 100 * mean(check_correct), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(pct_correct) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 1,
               caption = "Per-check accuracy. A check far below the rest is more
                          likely a bad item than a room full of inattentive
                          participants.")
```

## Side-bias check

`alpha_side` records which side the alphabetical order was shown on. It is
balanced 51/51 within each participant by construction, so this is a check that
the manipulation did what it claims, and that participants are not simply
clicking a preferred side.

```{r side-bias}
trials %>%
  group_by(alpha_side) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), prop_chose_alpha = mean(alpha_answer), .groups = "drop") %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

A large gap between the two rows means side is driving responses; the two
proportions should be close.

# Abstract preference

`AbsPref` is the Morgan & Levy abstract preference: a logistic over the weighted
constraint sum, defined in `load_human_data.R`. It is centred at 0.5 (`AbsPref_c`)
so the intercept is interpretable as the log-odds of choosing the alphabetical
order for an item with no abstract preference either way.

Two nuisance predictors ride along in every model below.

`trial_num_z` is position in the run, standardised, so practice and fatigue are
estimated rather than left in the residual. `alpha_side_c` is which side the
alphabetical order was drawn on, centred (left −0.5, right +0.5).

Both go in as **fixed** effects with by-participant random slopes, not as
grouping factors. `alpha_side` has two levels, and a two-level factor cannot be
a random-effect grouping term: there is no population of sides to generalise
over, and the variance is unidentifiable. The by-participant slope is the part
that is genuinely random, and it is the quantity of interest anyway, since it
asks whether individual people carry a side bias.

```{r control-terms}
## alpha_side is NA for anything collected before the counterbalancing was added
## (it was always on the left then). Leaving it in the formula would drop every
## such row without comment, so it only enters when it was logged and varies.
##
## It enters as the factor, not the centred numeric `alpha_side_c`, so that the
## contr.sum setting above actually applies to it. Under contr.sum the two
## levels are coded +1 and -1, which makes the coefficient *half* the
## left-to-right difference in log-odds; `alpha_side_c` (-0.5/+0.5) would have
## given the full difference. Both are in the data, so swap if you prefer that
## reading, but do not mix them across models.
ctrl_terms <- "trial_num_z"
side_usable <- !all(is.na(trials$alpha_side)) &&
               n_distinct(na.omit(trials$alpha_side)) > 1
if (side_usable) ctrl_terms <- c(ctrl_terms, "alpha_side")

if (!side_usable) {
  message("alpha_side not modelled: ",
          if (all(is.na(trials$alpha_side))) "absent from this data"
          else "only one side present")
}
ctrl_terms
```

```{r m-abspref}
f_abspref <- as.formula(paste(
  "alpha_answer ~ AbsPref_c +", paste(ctrl_terms, collapse = " + "),
  "+ (", paste(c("AbsPref_c", ctrl_terms), collapse = " + "), "| participant)",
  "+ (1 | Item)"
))

m_abspref <- brm(
  f_abspref,
  data = trials,
  family = bernoulli(link = "logit"),
  iter = ITER, warmup = WARMUP, chains = CHAINS, cores = CORES, seed = 964,
  file = "models/m_abspref"
)

fixef(m_abspref)
```

```{r side-and-trial}
## The two nuisance effects, read directly. A side coefficient far from zero
## means people favoured a position regardless of the ordering shown there.
if (side_usable) {
  ## Under contr.sum brms names the side coefficient b_alpha_side1.
  as_draws_df(m_abspref) %>%
    select(any_of(c("b_alpha_side1", "b_alpha_side_c", "b_trial_num_z"))) %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "term", values_to = "estimate") %>%
    group_by(term) %>%
    summarise(median = median(estimate),
              q2.5 = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
              q97.5 = quantile(estimate, 0.975),
              pct_above_zero = 100 * mean(estimate > 0),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    knitr::kable(digits = 3,
                 caption = "Side bias and position-in-run, on the log-odds scale.")
} else {
  knitr::kable(
    as_draws_df(m_abspref) %>%
      select(any_of("b_trial_num_z")) %>%
      summarise(median = median(b_trial_num_z),
                q2.5 = quantile(b_trial_num_z, 0.025),
                q97.5 = quantile(b_trial_num_z, 0.975)),
    digits = 3, caption = "Position-in-run. Side is not estimable in this data.")
}
```

```{r abspref-posterior}
## Proportion of posterior samples above zero, as in the source script.
as_draws_df(m_abspref) %>%
  select(b_Intercept, b_AbsPref_c) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "term", values_to = "estimate") %>%
  group_by(term) %>%
  summarise(median = median(estimate),
            q2.5 = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
            q97.5 = quantile(estimate, 0.975),
            pct_above_zero = 100 * mean(estimate > 0),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Item-level fit

Aggregating to one point per binomial is the clearest view of whether abstract
preference tracks what people actually do.

```{r plot-abspref, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
item_level <- trials %>%
  group_by(item_id, Item, AbsPref) %>%
  summarise(human_p = mean(alpha_answer), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(item_level, aes(x = AbsPref, y = human_p)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey80") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey80") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.6, 2.5), guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Abstract preference (AbsPref)",
       y = "Human preference for alphabetical order",
       caption = "Dashed line is identity. Point size is judgements per item.") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r abspref-cor}
with(item_level, tibble(
  pearson  = cor(AbsPref, human_p),
  spearman = cor(AbsPref, human_p, method = "spearman"),
  ## Does AbsPref at least get the direction right?
  direction_agreement = mean((AbsPref > 0.5) == (human_p > 0.5))
)) %>% knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

# Individual constraints

Every constraint that varies across these items, entered simultaneously. This
asks which constraints people are actually sensitive to, rather than assuming the
Morgan & Levy weighting.

```{r constraint-data}
## Continuous predictors are standardised so their coefficients are comparable
## with the +/-1 coded categorical ones. The categorical constraints are already
## on a common scale and are left alone.
trials_c <- trials %>%
  mutate(across(c(Freq, Len, Lapse), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x)), .names = "{.col}_z"))

constraint_terms <- c("Form", "Percept", "Culture", "Power", "Intense",
                      "Freq_z", "Len_z", "Lapse_z", "BStress")
```

```{r m-constraints}
## Random intercepts only. With nine predictors a full random-slope matrix is a
## 9x9 correlation to estimate and routinely fails to converge; the slope model
## below mirrors the CoNLL specification on the subset it used.
f_fixed <- as.formula(paste(
  "alpha_answer ~", paste(c(constraint_terms, ctrl_terms), collapse = " + "),
  "+ (", paste(ctrl_terms, collapse = " + "), "| participant) + (1 | Item)"
))

m_constraints <- brm(
  f_fixed,
  data = trials_c,
  family = bernoulli(link = "logit"),
  iter = ITER, warmup = WARMUP, chains = CHAINS, cores = CORES,
  file = "models/m_constraints"
)

fixef(m_constraints)
```

```{r m-constraints-slopes}
## The CoNLL specification: random slopes over the six constraints it modelled.
## Kept for comparability with that paper.
conll_terms <- c("Culture", "Power", "Freq_z", "Len_z", "Intense", "Percept")

f_slopes <- as.formula(paste(
  "alpha_answer ~", paste(c(conll_terms, ctrl_terms), collapse = " + "),
  "+ (", paste(c(conll_terms, ctrl_terms), collapse = " + "), "| participant)",
  "+ (1 | Item)"
))

m_constraints_slopes <- brm(
  f_slopes,
  data = trials_c,
  family = bernoulli(link = "logit"),
  iter = ITER, warmup = WARMUP, chains = CHAINS, cores = CORES,
  file = "models/m_constraints_slopes"
)

fixef(m_constraints_slopes)
```

```{r constraint-table}
constraint_summary <- as_draws_df(m_constraints) %>%
  select(starts_with("b_"), -b_Intercept) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "term", values_to = "estimate") %>%
  mutate(term = str_remove(term, "^b_")) %>%
  group_by(term) %>%
  summarise(median = median(estimate),
            q2.5 = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
            q97.5 = quantile(estimate, 0.975),
            pct_above_zero = 100 * mean(estimate > 0),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(median)))

knitr::kable(constraint_summary, digits = 3)
```

```{r plot-constraints, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
constraint_summary %>%
  mutate(term = fct_reorder(term, median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = median, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = q2.5, xmax = q97.5)) +
  labs(x = "Coefficient (log-odds of choosing the alphabetical order)",
       y = NULL,
       caption = "Points are posterior medians with 95% credible intervals.") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Fitted weights against Morgan & Levy's

Do the constraint weights people show here match the ones AbsPref assumes? The
two are on different scales, so the comparison is about relative ordering and
sign, not absolute magnitude.

```{r weights-vs-ml, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
ml <- tibble(term = names(ML_WEIGHTS), ml_weight = as.numeric(ML_WEIGHTS)) %>%
  filter(term != "Intercept")

constraint_summary %>%
  mutate(base = str_remove(term, "_z$")) %>%
  inner_join(ml, by = c("base" = "term")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ml_weight, y = median)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5)) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = term), size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Morgan & Levy weight (used by AbsPref)",
       y = "Fitted weight in this study") +
  theme_bw()
```

# Model comparison

Does knowing the individual constraints buy anything over the single AbsPref
summary? Both are fit to the same rows, so LOO is comparable.

```{r loo}
m_abspref          <- add_criterion(m_abspref, "loo")
m_constraints      <- add_criterion(m_constraints, "loo")
loo_compare(m_abspref, m_constraints)
```

A large advantage for `m_constraints` means people weight the constraints
differently from Morgan & Levy's fixed weighting; a small one means AbsPref
already captures most of what the constraints explain.
